news.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at $83 a share, above the marketed range
news.summary: Anthropic set its IPO price at $83, above the $70-$78 range it had marketed to investors, implying a valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion. Reports of the total amount raised differ between outlets, but it is described as a record listing.

news.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon, a 1M-token model at $3/$15 per million tokens
news.summary: Google's new Gemini 4 Neon has a one-million-token context window and costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Google pitches it as competitive with rival flagship models for less money, and it ranked first on one coding-agent index.

news.title: Genie 4 reaches Project Genie for AI Ultra subscribers, with chainable worlds
news.summary: Google DeepMind's Project Genie now runs on the Genie 4 world model for eligible AI Ultra subscribers. Users can chain generated worlds together and browse a community gallery to remix other people's creations.

news.title: Palo Alto Networks to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion
news.summary: The cybersecurity company agreed to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at about $4.5 billion. It is the latest large AI purchase by a security vendor.

news.title: OpenAI says its models improved AMD GPU designs by up to 14%
news.summary: OpenAI reports that its models were used in AMD's chip design work and produced GPU design improvements of up to 14%. It is a concrete example of AI labs applying their own models to the hardware they run on.

news.title: Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress holds first all-hands since Huang's exit
news.summary: Colette Kress addressed Nvidia staff for the first time since Jensen Huang resigned, acknowledging a difficult period. The meeting included news of pay raises for employees.

news.title: Moody's cuts Nvidia's outlook to stable, citing no formal succession plan
news.summary: The ratings agency lowered Nvidia's outlook from positive to stable after Huang's resignation. Moody's pointed to the lack of a formal succession plan at the world's most valuable chipmaker.

news.title: Cloudflare releases open weights for its Clairic extraction models
news.summary: Cloudflare published open weights for Clairic (27B) and Clairic-flash (9B). The models pull typed data out of text, images and PDFs rather than writing free-form replies.

news.title: IEA warns datacentre emissions could rise 70% by 2030
news.summary: A new International Energy Agency report projects that carbon emissions from datacentres will grow by about 70% by the end of the decade. AI workloads are a major driver of the expected increase in power demand.

news.title: Singapore's central bank warns AI agents could speed up money flows
news.summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore said AI agents acting for customers could move funds much faster than people do. That could raise liquidity risks for banks during periods of stress.

news.title: Maryland students sue after AI gun alert flagged a bag of Doritos
news.summary: Four students filed a lawsuit after an AI gun-detection system mistook a snack bag for a weapon and police detained them. The case adds to scrutiny of AI surveillance tools in schools.

papers.title: PanDWM: Panoramic 4D Driving World Models
papers.tldr: PanDWM imagines a self-driving car's future surroundings as one stitched 360° panorama instead of six separate camera videos, which gives smoother, more consistent scenes and runs about 17 times faster than the slow model it learned from.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
PanDWM is an AI that imagines what a car's cameras will see next, drawing the whole 360° view as one continuous panorama and then turning it into a 3D scene that changes over time.

## Background you need
A driving world model is a video generator for self-driving research. You give it a road layout (where the lanes and other cars are) plus a few past frames, and it predicts the next seconds of video. Companies use these fake-but-realistic videos to train and test driving software without risky real drives. Most test cars carry six cameras that together cover the full circle around the car.

## The problem
Today's world models usually generate six separate videos, one per camera. A truck that crosses from the front camera into the side camera gets split across two images made separately. The halves often don't line up: the truck may change shape or colour at the seam. Models add special "cross-view" tricks to fix this, but the cut is still there. These models are also slow. They clean up each clip with 50 to 100 passes through a large network, taking 16 to 90 seconds per frame. And they are trained on real past frames but must run on their own imperfect output, so errors pile up over long videos.

## The idea
Instead of six photos taped together, PanDWM paints one wide strip, like a panoramic photo from a phone. Camera boundaries now fall in the middle of a single image, so nothing gets cut. A second trick is "teacher and student": a slow, careful model teaches a fast one, like an apprentice learning to sketch in four strokes what the master paints in fifty.

## How it works
1. **Stitch the views.** The six camera images are mapped onto one 360° band. Every pixel remembers which camera and viewing direction it came from. The band is split into two overlapping halves so each camera boundary sits inside one half.
2. **Train a careful teacher.** A large image-generation network learns to predict 16 future frames from 3 past ones, guided by the road layout. It needs 100 network passes per chunk of video.
3. **Distil a fast student.** A student copy learns to reach the same result in just four passes. Crucially, it practises on its own generated history, not only on real footage. That way it learns to recover from its own small mistakes over long drives.
4. **Keep it realistic.** Extra "judge" networks penalise output that looks fake or flickers between frames.
5. **Lift to 3D.** A separate decoder turns each panoramic frame into a cloud of tiny coloured blobs (3D Gaussians) placed along each camera ray. Static blobs from nearby frames fill holes, producing a 4D scene: 3D space plus time.

## Results
Tests used nuScenes, a public dataset of city driving in Boston and Singapore. Compared with five recent multi-camera models, PanDWM had the best image quality score (FID 10.1, against 17.2 for the next best; lower is better). It also had the best video consistency scores (FVD), for example 37.4 against 46.0 for the next best. It produces a frame in about 2 seconds, versus 16 to 90 seconds for the baselines, so it is 8 to 46 times faster. Against its own teacher, it uses 25 times fewer network passes and runs about 17 times faster. Image quality stayed essentially equal and the video consistency score improved by 22–25%. On 19.5-second drives, the student drifted less than the teacher in every later stretch.

## Why it matters
Self-driving teams need huge amounts of realistic, varied test footage. A generator that is faster and keeps the full surround view consistent makes simulated testing cheaper and more trustworthy. The 4D output could also feed simulators that need real 3D geometry, not just flat video.

## Caveats
Everything was tested on one dataset, nuScenes. Scores were measured in the panoramic view, which required stitching the baselines' outputs too, and that choice can affect comparisons. The ablation studies were short training runs on a small set of scenes. Two seconds per frame is still far from real time.

## Key terms
- **World model:** an AI that predicts how a scene will look in the future.
- **Panorama band:** one wide image covering the full circle around the car.
- **Distillation:** training a fast model to copy a slower, better one.
- **FID / FVD:** standard scores for how realistic images and videos look; lower is better.
- **3D Gaussians:** tiny fuzzy coloured blobs used to build a 3D scene that can be viewed from any angle.

papers.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
papers.tldr: DNeo is a small helper model that guesses many upcoming words at once for a big language model, and by reading the big model's internal signals more faithfully and remembering its own rejected guesses, it makes text generation about 1.3 times faster than the previous best helper.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
DNeo is a small "guessing" model that drafts many words at once for a large language model, and it guesses better because it reads the large model's internal state more carefully and learns from its own wrong guesses.

## Background you need
Large language models write one token (a word or word piece) at a time, and each token needs a full pass through the huge network. Speculative decoding speeds this up. A small drafter model proposes several tokens, and the big target model checks them all in one pass, keeping the ones it agrees with. A parallel drafter goes further and proposes a whole block of tokens in a single step. The more guesses get accepted, the bigger the speed-up.

## The problem
Good drafters peek at the target model's hidden features, the numbers inside the big model that summarise what it is thinking. The authors find three weaknesses in how current parallel drafters use those features. First, the features get squashed through mixing layers that distort them. Second, drafters forget what happened last round: when the target rejects a guess, that information is thrown away. Third, they sample the target's layers at even spacing, which can skip the most useful ones. Each weakness means fewer accepted guesses and slower chatbots.

## The idea
Think of a junior writer drafting sentences for a senior editor. A smart junior reads the editor's notes closely instead of a blurry photocopy. They also remember which suggestions the editor crossed out, so they don't repeat them. DNeo gives the drafter both habits.

## How it works
1. **Better feature reading.** A light component called Mixture-of-Features Attention blends features from seven chosen layers of the target model. It keeps them clean instead of distorting them, and one shared blend is reused throughout the drafter.
2. **Rejection memory.** Features from tokens the target just rejected become a memory the drafter can look at when making its next guess.
3. **Smarter layer choice.** Instead of evenly spaced layers, the drafter uses a hand-picked, uneven set of target layers that carry more useful signal.
4. **Small local links.** Short convolutions (filters that look at neighbouring positions) let each guessed token see its immediate neighbours, and a final head conditions each guess on the previous one.
5. **One pass.** A five-layer drafter produces a block of up to 15 guessed tokens in a single forward pass. The target then verifies them.

## Results
The paper reports about 1.3 times faster generation than the previous best parallel drafter, DFlash-2, with the same drafter size and no loss in output quality. The released model pairs DNeo with Qwen3-4B, a 4-billion-parameter open model, on a single H100 graphics card. There it accepts about 4.5 tokens per target pass on average. Decoding runs 2.96 times faster than plain one-token-at-a-time generation in the SGLang serving system, and 3.37 times faster in the Hugging Face Transformers library. In practice, an answer that took 3 seconds to write would take about 1. Tests covered maths, coding, science questions and chat benchmarks.

## Why it matters
Speed is cost. Anyone serving language models, from chat apps to coding tools, pays for every pass of the big model. A drafter that gets more guesses accepted cuts waiting time and hardware bills without changing the big model's answers.

## Caveats
Results come from one fairly small target model and one card type, with short prompts and fixed 512-token outputs. Speed-ups depend on the task, and the authors note this. Batch size was one, so gains when serving many users at once are not shown. The drafter must be trained separately for each target model.

## Key terms
- **Token:** a word or word piece that a language model reads or writes.
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model guesses ahead and a big model checks the guesses in one go.
- **Drafter:** the small guessing model.
- **Hidden features:** internal numbers inside a network that summarise its current understanding.
- **Acceptance length:** how many guessed tokens the big model keeps per check.

papers.title: Multi-Branch Transformer
papers.tldr: Instead of only stacking layers deeper or wider, the Multi-Branch Transformer runs several stacks of layers side by side and merges them, matching a standard model trained with about 20% more compute while decoding up to 51% faster.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The Multi-Branch Transformer splits the middle of a language model into several parallel lanes of layers, then merges them, which gives similar or better quality and noticeably faster text generation.

## Background you need
A transformer, the design behind most chatbots, is a tall stack of identical blocks. Each block has attention (looking back at earlier words) and a feed-forward part (processing each word). To make a model better, people usually make it deeper (more blocks) or wider (bigger blocks). When generating text, each block also keeps a KV cache: the model's short-term memory of everything it has already read.

## The problem
Depth is slow at generation time, because block 20 must wait for block 19 to finish for every new word. Width makes each step heavier. The KV cache also grows with every block and every word, so memory often limits how many users a server can handle. Almost all designs keep whole blocks in one sequential line, and few people have asked whether running whole blocks side by side could be a better use of the same budget.

## The idea
Picture a factory. A single long assembly line has many stations in a row. A Multi-Branch Transformer keeps a shared start and a shared finish, but in the middle it splits the work into two to four shorter lines running at the same time. Then it combines their output. The product passes fewer stations in sequence, so it comes out sooner.

## How it works
1. **Shared start.** Words are turned into vectors and pass through a few ordinary shared blocks.
2. **Parallel branches.** The signal then goes into two to four independent branches. Each is its own short stack of blocks with its own weights, and the branches run at the same time.
3. **Merge.** Each branch's output is normalised, the outputs are joined side by side, and a simple linear layer squeezes them back to the normal size.
4. **Shared finish.** A few more shared blocks produce the next-word prediction.
5. **Joint-KV.** Rather than each branch keeping its own memory, branches at the same depth share one KV cache built from all their inputs. This saves memory and lets the system batch the branches into one attention call on the GPU.

## Results
Models ranged from 0.8 to 2.1 billion total parameters, using a mixture-of-experts design (only part of the network is active per word). They were trained on an educational web text dataset. The best two-branch version matched a standard transformer trained with about 1.23 times as much compute. That is like getting a 23% bigger training budget for free. Joint-KV versions with two to four branches matched standard models trained with 1.16 to 1.26 times the compute. The KV cache shrank by 19–34%, and decoding on one H200 GPU was up to 51% faster. A four-branch model with 24 blocks needed only 12 sequential steps, versus 16 for the standard model. Branches worked best when placed in the middle layers.

## Why it matters
Faster decoding and a smaller memory footprint mean cheaper serving and more users per GPU. Because the change is architectural, it can stack with other speed tricks such as quantisation or speculative decoding. It also opens a new design axis, "how many branches", alongside depth and width.

## Caveats
The largest model tested had about 2 billion parameters, far smaller than frontier models. Joint-KV must be built in during training, so existing models can't be converted. The standard baselines got careful learning-rate tuning, while branched models reused one setting. That should favour the baselines, but it still complicates comparisons. Speed was measured on one GPU type and a few workloads.

## Key terms
- **Transformer block:** one layer of attention plus processing; models stack many of them.
- **Branch:** a separate stack of blocks that runs in parallel with others.
- **KV cache:** stored notes about earlier words so the model doesn't reread them.
- **Mixture-of-experts:** a design where each word uses only some of the network's sub-parts.
- **Decoding throughput:** how many words per second a model can generate.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.tldr: AscendGYM is a test suite that checks whether AI coding agents can speed up real low-level code on Huawei's Ascend AI chips, and it scores them on how much faster the code gets relative to how many tokens they spend getting there.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
AscendGYM is a benchmark that measures how well AI coding agents can make existing chip code run faster on Huawei's Ascend AI processors, while also counting how much the agent spent to get there.

## Background you need
A kernel is a small, highly tuned program that does one heavy maths job, such as normalising numbers or computing attention, directly on an AI chip. Ascend NPUs (neural processing units) are Huawei's AI accelerators, playing the role Nvidia GPUs play elsewhere. Writing fast kernels is a rare, slow skill. AI coding agents, language models that edit, compile and test code in a loop, are now being asked to do it. Each loop costs tokens (pieces of text the model reads and writes), and tokens cost money.

## The problem
Existing Ascend benchmarks mostly ask agents to write a kernel from scratch. Real engineering work is different: you already have a working kernel and need it faster for the exact shapes and data types your model uses. Existing tests also usually report only the final speed-up. They ignore whether the agent burned ten times more tokens to get a slightly better result, or found the gain late after a long, expensive search.

## The idea
Think of hiring a mechanic to tune a car. You care how much faster it goes, but also how big the bill is and how quickly they found the fix. AscendGYM grades agents like that: speed-up, discounted by the token bill spent before each improvement arrived.

## How it works
1. **Pick real bottlenecks.** The team profiled real training and inference jobs and chose 48 kernels that eat significant time. For example, one normalisation step takes about 9% of compute in a small Qwen model's prompt-reading phase.
2. **Three difficulty batches.** 17 simple kernels limited by memory access, 17 multi-step kernels such as normalisation and quantisation, and 14 complex attention and fused kernels.
3. **Real test cases.** Each case records the model, phase, hardware setup, tensor shapes and number formats it came from, so a gain in the benchmark is a gain in that real job.
4. **A safe sandbox.** A system called AscendForge compiles each candidate, checks it gives correct answers, and times it.
5. **Two modes and a cost-aware score.** Agents can be tested with their own harness (the tool loop around the model, such as Claude Code or Codex CLI) or with a built-in one. The Speedup-Token Score rewards the final verified speed-up and subtracts points for gains that only came after much of the token budget was spent.

## Results
The first round tested only the 17 easiest kernels, with budgets of 10, 20 and 50 million tokens. About 70% of agent-and-harness combinations reached less than 1.2 times average speed-up. In other words, most agents shaved off less than a sixth of the run time even on the simplest tasks. The choice of harness and the token budget changed outcomes a lot, not just the underlying model. Pass rates and average speed-up sometimes pointed in different directions, which the new score helps untangle.

## Why it matters
AI chips outside the Nvidia ecosystem have far fewer expert kernel writers, so automated tuning could matter a lot there. A benchmark tied to real workloads and real costs tells teams whether an agent is worth paying for. The cost-aware scoring idea could be reused for GPU kernel benchmarks too.

## Caveats
Only 17 of the 48 kernels have results so far; the harder attention and fused kernels are pending. The scoring weights are design choices that change rankings. Everything is specific to Huawei's Ascend hardware and software stack. Our summary relied on secondary write-ups of the paper, which did not list every model tested.

## Key terms
- **Kernel:** a small, fast program that runs one maths operation on an AI chip.
- **NPU:** neural processing unit, a chip built for AI maths.
- **Harness:** the tool loop that lets a language model edit, run and test code.
- **Speed-up:** how many times faster the new code is than the original.
- **Token budget:** the maximum text an agent may read and write during the task.

papers.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
papers.tldr: ForceHarness lets off-the-shelf AI models like GPT and Claude control a robot arm using touch and force, through ready-made force tools and plain-language physics readings, lifting real-robot success from 3% to 90% with no extra training.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
ForceHarness gives big off-the-shelf AI models a sense of touch for robot control, by handing them force tools and translating raw force signals into plain physical facts they can reason about.

## Background you need
Frontier multimodal models, large AIs that read images and text, can already steer robot arms by looking at camera pictures and calling simple motion commands. A harness is the software layer between the model and the robot that offers it tools. Many jobs depend on force, though: how hard you press, whether something is heavy, whether a peg has dropped into a hole. Cameras can't see force. These models are also frozen and reached only through an API, so you can't retrain them.

## The problem
Robot policies that use force today need many human demonstrations per task and weight training, which is impossible with API-only models. Simple fixes, like pasting raw force numbers into the prompt or asking the model to write force-control code, work poorly. Contact happens in milliseconds, but a model takes seconds to reply. And a stream of raw numbers is hard for a language model to interpret.

## The idea
Think of a surgeon working with a skilled assistant. The surgeon says "hold this with gentle pressure" rather than adjusting every muscle. The assistant then reports back "it's soft tissue, about this firm". ForceHarness is that assistant. Fast force control runs underneath the model, and results come back as physical facts with error bars.

## How it works
1. **Sense force.** The system estimates force at the hand from a wrist sensor, or from the arm's joint torque readings if no wrist sensor exists. It zeroes itself at rest before each reading.
2. **Self-stopping force tools.** The model gets twelve force tools in five groups: make contact, hold a force, search and seat, turn under load, and measure. Each runs its own fast control loop and stops by itself on contact, on a force limit, or on a timeout, then holds still while the model thinks. For example, a search tool presses down while spiralling until a part drops into its hole.
3. **Translate physics.** Simple fixed estimators turn force traces into quantities like mass, contact height, stiffness and friction, each with an uncertainty and warning flags.
4. **Model in the loop.** Each turn, the model reads the task, its tool menu, history and latest readings, then calls one tool. It decides if a result is good enough.
5. **Safety guards.** Hard limits on force, speed and workspace apply no matter what the model asks for.

## Results
On a real Franka robot arm with no wrist sensor, across six tasks, GPT-6 Astra succeeded in 2 of 60 attempts without force tools (3%). With ForceHarness it succeeded in 54 of 60 (90%). Tasks such as bottle sorting went from 0 of 10 to 10 of 10. On the public ForceBench simulation suite, success rose from 70% to 87.5%. The best trained robot policy scored 35%. On the authors' new HiddenPhys benchmark, seven tasks with hidden properties like mass, success went from 62% to 96%. A hand-written expert controller scored 97%. Asking the model to write one force-control program upfront reached only 23%, versus 91% for turn-by-turn tool use.

## Why it matters
This means general AI models could handle contact-rich jobs, such as assembly, sorting or checking whether a lid is tight, with no demonstrations and no training. Robot makers can upgrade by swapping in a newer model, keeping the same harness.

## Caveats
Each model call adds seconds of pause, so fast reactive tasks are out of reach. The fixed tool menu limits what new motions are possible. Several detailed comparisons were only run in simulation, and some tool settings were tuned on the same benchmark seeds used for testing.

## Key terms
- **Frozen model:** an AI used as-is, without further training.
- **Harness:** the software layer that offers a model tools and feeds back results.
- **Force primitive:** a ready-made, self-stopping force action like "press until contact".
- **Impedance control:** a way of moving a robot so it behaves like a spring, giving way gently on contact.
- **Zero-shot:** doing a task with no examples or training for it.

papers.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
papers.tldr: Gamer is a vision-language model trained on thousands of hours of real keyboard-and-mouse play that watches the screen and plays long 2D and 3D games in real time, nearly tripling the score of a top general model on unseen mini-games.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Gamer is an AI that watches a game screen and presses keys and moves the mouse in real time, finishing long quests in 3D open-world games much like a skilled human player.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action model is a language model that also takes in images and outputs actions, here keyboard and mouse commands. Games are a demanding test: the screen changes constantly, tasks take hours, and the agent must remember what it did earlier. A context window is how much recent history a model can hold in mind at once. Reinforcement learning (RL) is training by trial and error, with rewards for success.

## The problem
General chatbots with vision can describe a game screen, but they are slow and lose track over long tasks. Many game agents also cheat a little by reading the game's internal code state, which real users and robots can't do. Long quests overflow the context window. Small mistakes snowball over hundreds of steps. And rewards are rare: you might only learn you succeeded at the end of a long quest.

## The idea
Gamer learns like a person who watched thousands of hours of others playing, then practised. Most of the time it acts on instinct. It only stops to think at real decision points, like a driver who doesn't deliberate on every turn of the wheel. When its memory fills up, it writes itself a short summary note and carries on.

## How it works
1. **Watch a lot of play.** The base model is further trained on tens of thousands of hours of keyboard-and-mouse recordings from games and simulated worlds, so it learns how actions change what's on screen.
2. **Learn to follow instructions.** It is then tuned on about 1,000 curated hours of the game Honkai: Star Rail, with about 1.2 million reasoning notes and 223,000 memory notes added by an annotation pipeline.
3. **Think only when needed.** "Sparse thinking" training teaches it to act directly on routine steps and reason briefly only at hard choices, saving time.
4. **Practise with rewards.** A multi-turn RL method splits long tasks into segments linked by memory notes. It compares several attempts at the same segment, so credit goes to the decisions that helped.
5. **Run in real time.** It sees the screen five times a second and issues about 30 small control actions per second. A custom serving engine reuses its memory between frames and runs many games at once.

## Results
On a side quest held out from training, Gamer completed 83.6% of 55 checkpoints after RL, up from 69.1% before RL. On 40 unseen mini-game levels across seven game types, it scored 49.7%. The strongest general model listed, GPT-6.1 Sol, scored 17.1%, so Gamer did nearly three times better. The authors report handling over 95% of challenges across several main storylines of Honkai: Star Rail. They also report more than 20 times lower response delay in their setup. Training in real time learned faster than training at a slow 0.6 frames per second.

## Why it matters
Game studios could use such agents to test levels, find bugs or balance difficulty without armies of human testers. More broadly, an agent that only sees pixels and uses a keyboard and mouse could operate any computer program. The same skills of acting fast, remembering and planning over long horizons also matter for robots.

## Caveats
The test quests were new, but the game itself was in training, so this isn't a fully unseen game. Gains from pre-training were limited in very different worlds. The study doesn't separate how much each ingredient (sparse thinking, memory, RL) contributes. A reviewer also flagged a small inconsistency in one results table. Strong claims about other 3D games come without detailed numbers.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language-action model:** an AI that reads images and text and outputs actions.
- **Context window:** how much recent history a model can keep in mind.
- **Reinforcement learning:** learning by trial and error with rewards.
- **Long-horizon task:** a goal that takes many steps or a long time to finish.
- **Sparse thinking:** reasoning only at important moments, not every step.
